data.title: Bank of Canada's Growth Outlook Appears 'Very Tenuous' — Market Talk
data.description: GDP data for Canada indicates that the solid growth envisaged by the Bank of Canada into 2027 "remains very tenuous," says Carl Gomez, chief economist at Toronto-based Centurion Asset Management. Via a post on LinkedIn, Gomez says GDP in Canada may struggle to grow over 1% annualized in 3Q, whereas BOC forecast 2%. "The takeaway," Gomez says, "is that the BOC's rate-hiking cycle is unlikely to be a protracted one," and will have to monitor incoming data to before tightening financial conditions further. He anticipates one more BOC rate hike in early 2027, although he says he doesn't expect policymakers "going much further unless the actual data warrants it."(paul.vieira@wsj.com; @paulvieira)

data.title: BofA's Merrill Lynch to end use of proxy advisers starting 2027
data.description:
Bank of America's Merrill Lynch unit no longer plans to use proxy advisers starting 2027, according to a document on Friday, as US big banks move to handle shareholder voting internally.

Proxy advisers and large fund managers have for years attracted criticism from conservatives and some business leaders, who argue such firms often recommend votes against boardroom decisions or directors and place too much emphasis on climate and social issues.

Here are some other details:

  • Under the revamped proxy voting framework, Merrill's clients will not have the option to delegate proxy voting authority to proxy firm Institutional Shareholder Services (ISS) starting January.

  • Merrill will assume and accept proxy voting authority for clients who had delegated it to ISS and do not opt out of the transition by December 15.

  • Proxy advisory firms review shareholder proposals and corporate governance issues and provide voting recommendations to institutional investors ahead of annual shareholder meetings.

  • JPMorgan Chase's asset management division earlier this year moved to cut ties with proxy advisers in the US, Reuters reported, a move the bank had described as an industry first.

  • In 2025, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at increasing oversight of the proxy advisory industry on grounds that top firms often "advance and prioritize radical politically-motivated agendas."

data.title: ZIONS BANCORPORATION'S BOARD ANNOUNCES APPROVAL OF SHARE REPURCHASE AND DECLARES DIVIDENDS ON COMMON AND PREFERRED STOCK
data.description:
SALT LAKE CITY, Oct. 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Zions Bancorporation, N.A. () announced today that its board of directors has authorized share repurchases of up to $72 million of the company's common stock for the fourth quarter of 2026 as part of the company's previously authorized share repurchase target for 2026 of $300 million. The timing and amounts of any such actions will depend on market conditions, regulatory requirements, and other factors or uncertainties and may be updated at the discretion of the board.

The board also declared a regular quarterly dividend of $0.48 per common share, payable November 19, 2026, to shareholders of record at the close of business on November 12, 2026.

Additionally, the board declared the regular quarterly cash dividend on the company's Series A perpetual preferred shares (; CUSIP: 98973A104). The cash dividends on the preferred shares are payable December 15, 2026, to shareholders of record on December 1, 2026.

Zions Bancorporation, N.A. is one of the nation's premier financial services companies with approximately $89 billion of total assets at December 31, 2025, and annual net revenue of $3.4 billion in 2025. Zions operates under local management teams and distinct brands in 11 western states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Idaho, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Texas, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. The Bank is a consistent recipient of national and state-wide customer survey awards in small- and middle-market banking, as well as a leader in public finance advisory services and Small Business Administration lending. In addition, Zions is included in the S&P MidCap 400 and NASDAQ Financial 100 indices. Investor information and links to local banking brands can be accessed at www.zionsbancorporation.com.

SOURCE Zions Bancorporation

data.title: Mexico's Pemex 3Q Net Loss Shrinks on Higher Sales, Operating Gains
data.description:
By Anthony Harrup

MEXICO CITY--State-owned oil company Petroleos Mexicanos posted a narrower net loss in the third quarter than in the year-earlier period as sales and operating results improved.

Pemex reported a loss of 10.8 billion Mexican pesos ($574.5 million) for the July-September period, compared with a loss of MXN61.24 billion in the year-earlier quarter.

Higher sales and lower fixed-asset impairment costs were offset in part by higher product purchases, higher taxes and duties, and a foreign-exchange loss, the company said Friday.

"Pemex continued strengthening its performance through increased levels of production, refining, and marketing of fuels," the company said.

Third-quarter sales rose 28.5% from a year earlier to MXN486.78 billion, driven largely by higher domestic fuel sales and favorable prices for petroleum products. Operating profit was MXN97.59 billion, compared with a MXN12.88 billion year-earlier operating loss.

Production of crude oil and condensates slipped 0.4% to 1.64 million barrels a day, while natural-gas production rose 7.9% to 5.017 billion cubic feet a day. Pemex refineries processed 1.14 million barrels a day of crude oil, the most since 2014 and up 14% from the year-earlier quarter. Production of petroleum products rose 16% to 1.16 million barrels a day.

Pemex's debt was $77.6 billion at the end of September, practically unchanged from June and down 8.9% from the end of 2025.

data.title: Britain approves 2 gigawatt undersea power cable
data.description:
Britain has approved development of a 2 gigawatt undersea electricity connection linking Suffolk in the East of England and Kent in the South East of the country, capable of carrying enough electricity to power about 2 million homes, it said on Friday.

  • Britain’s Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said the project will help strengthen the country's energy security, making the power network more resilient and reducing wasted energy, helping to bring down costs.

  • The 138km project is being developed by National Grid while the subsea cable being used will be manufactured by Sumitomo Electric at its £350 million factory at Port of Nigg in Scotland, National Grid said in a separate statement.

  • Construction is expected to begin in early 2027, with the project expected to be complete by the 2030s, subject to detailed construction planning and construction agreements, National Grid said.

  • Britain needs to invest about £89 billion through the 2030s to overhaul its power grid, to help strengthen ageing infrastructure, meet an expected increase in demand and accommodate more renewable power, the National Energy System Operator said earlier this year.

data.title: Weil's meltdown sparks scramble for firm's 700 associates
data.description:
By Karen Sloan

The rapid dissolution of major Wall Street law firm Weil, Gotshal & Manges has left its nearly 700 associates scrambling to find new positions, including some who started as new associates just last week.

Weil's strong reputation and a healthy hiring market could bolster prospects for experienced associates in corporate practices, legal recruiters and consultants said. Rival firm Gibson Dunn is already expected to hire 20 associates from Weil's London private funds team as part of a 40-lawyer move.

Unlike law firm partners with a book of client business who can count on being courted, the associates who support them are seen as more fungible and can't necessarily tag along when their bosses and mentors find new homes. The options may be especially limited for Weil's junior associates, particularly in litigation practices, recruiters said.

“Litigation sees less movement, and my concern is that there simply may not be enough open seats for everyone,” said Evan Fox, a recruiter with Long Ridge Partners.

Weil’s leadership told partners on Wednesday that the 1,200-lawyer firm plans to wind down its operations following an exodus of partners, with a formal vote expected in the coming days. The dissolution marks an abrupt end for one of the most prominent and profitable US law firms.

The firm’s associates and staff were told they will continue to receive pay for 90 days and receive bonuses at the end of 2026, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

Weil told associates after the dissolution announcement that it would "do what we can to help you take the next step in your careers," in a message that was first reported by legal online publication Above the Law. Associates elsewhere have flooded Reddit and other online platforms with offers to split recruiting fees for Weil associates who join their firms.

Online legal job board Lateral Hub created a dedicated page for Weil associates to submit applications to interested firms. It listed 33 participating firms as of Friday morning, including Cooley; Fried Frank; and Wilson Sonsini.

According to Weil's website, its largest cohort of associates are in its private equity practice, at 134, followed by complex commercial litigation at 89, banking and finance at 76, and restructuring at 75.

LESSONS FROM DEWEY

Current Weil associates can take some solace from the aftermath of Dewey & LeBoeuf's collapse. Many associates landed on their feet following that firm’s 2012 bankruptcy, said Robert Kamins, a law firm consultant with Vertex Advisors.

“We’ve seen this movie before,” Kamins said of Dewey’s demise. “You saw a mass scramble of people needing to find new homes due to something totally unexpected and out of their control.”

A 2023 study by University of Texas law professor Andrew Granato found that about 50% of Dewey’s associates quickly landed jobs at other Am Law 100 firms, while 80% of Dewey partners became either partner or senior counsel at those highly profitable firms.

Among the former Dewey associates who landed at large firms, half secured their new positions through “cluster hires” as groups of partners moved together to other firms, Granato found.

Granato said in an interview on Thursday that his research suggests Dewey’s dissolution accelerated typical large-firm attrition by several years. Partners brought over high-billing associates on track for partnership to their new firms, he said, while associates with lower hours and potential plans to leave Big Law in several years went elsewhere.

Individual Weil partners will be a key resource for associates, Fox said, either by bringing them along to new firms or personally recommending them.

But law firm recruiter Kevin Cipolli of Voy Legal cautioned against associates relying too heavily on partners for their next career move, noting that firms might not have capacity for more associates, especially as usage of legal AI tools rises.

'A REALLY TOUGH SPOT'

Current law students who were headed to Weil as summer associates and first-year associates face particular challenges, as competitor firms have already filled those available positions, according to law school career services officers.

“It’s a really tough spot that none of them thought they were going to be in,” said Amy Jones Mattock, assistant dean of career services at Georgetown University Law Center, which has 33 current students and 2026 graduates who are at or headed to Weil.

In addition to Georgetown, the law schools at Harvard, Columbia, New York University and Northwestern told Reuters they are connecting with students headed to Weil and alumni at the firm to help them navigate their next steps.

Second-year students poised to be summer associates at Weil this year could opt to seek out opportunities at midsized firms or in government as many large firms have already filled their summer classes, Georgetown's Mattock said. Third-year law students may find more opportunities in large firms as firms look to plug gaps in their incoming associate classes, she said.

Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law is advising alumni associates at Weil about their next steps and developing individualized job search strategies for its students who were headed to the firm, said assistant dean for career services David Diamond. The school’s alumni at other firms are also stepping up with offers to help, he said.

Cipolli said rival firms have wasted no time reaching out to recruiters, himself included, looking for potential Weil associate hires.

“In a normal market, a Weil associate is going to be compelling and is going to have options,” he said. “There’s just going to be more competition right now.”
